paper_title: How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: Frequency formats
focus: Gigerenzer and Hoffrage (1995), Bayesian algorithms. Explain Bayes' theorem for a screening test using a base rate, a hit rate and a false-alarm rate. Show the posterior probability of disease given a positive test and the matching natural frequencies out of 1000 people. Let the learner change the three rates and switch between probability format and natural-frequency format. Guide them through a rare disease with an accurate test and a test whose hit rate equals its false-alarm rate. Check that the posterior equals the base rate when the hit rate equals the false-alarm rate and that both formats give the same posterior; handle a base rate of zero.
excerpt: (paraphrased) In the standard probability format a problem gives the base rate p(H) of a hypothesis, the hit rate p(D|H) and the false-alarm rate p(D|not-H). Bayes' theorem gives the posterior p(H|D) = p(H)p(D|H) / [p(H)p(D|H) + p(not-H)p(D|not-H)] (Equation 1). The authors argue that the same information can instead be presented as natural frequencies obtained by natural sampling, for example: of 1000 people, 10 have the disease; of these 10, 8 test positive; of the 990 without the disease, 95 also test positive. The posterior is then simply the number of true positives divided by all positives, 8/(8+95) (Equation 2), which requires fewer computational steps. Both formats are mathematically equivalent; the paper reports that people reason more accurately with natural frequencies.
